mainTopic: מעשר בהמה: when distant flocks join, why the יַרְדֵּן divides them, and the 'sources' of rivers, blood and water
overview: This amud deals with מעשר בהמה and when flocks in different places join together to make a count of ten. A ברייתא seems to refute רב, who needs five animals in the middle, but שמואל reads it in a way that fits רב. רב פפא adds that according to שמואל even the shepherd or his tools in the middle join the flocks, and רב אשי's question about the shepherd's dog ends in תיקו. The גמרא then turns to רבי מאיר's rule that the יַרְדֵּן separates flocks. רבי אמי says this is because the animals cannot cross, so a bridge would join them. רבי חייא בר אבא in the name of רבי יוחנן says instead that a פסוק makes the יַרְדֵּן a border, and רבי אמי's view is left with a קשיא. The גמרא brings a dispute between תנאים on whether the יַרְדֵּן is ארץ כנען, and teaches that the river is only called יַרְדֵּן from בית ירחו southward, a rule that matters for מעשר בהמה. It ends with רב כהנא's three 'sources': פמייס for the יַרְדֵּן, the liver for blood, and the פרת for all water, with a challenge about the פרת that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to refute רב
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that two groups of five, in כפר חנניה and כפר עותנאי, join only if there is one animal in ציפורי between them. That suggests one animal in the middle is enough, which goes against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged this: If someone had five animals in כפר חנניה and five in כפר עותנאי, they do not join together unless he also has one in ציפורי. This is a refutation of רב!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to attack רב. רב said there must be five animals in the middle to join two distant flocks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: כפר חנניה and כפר עותנאי are too far apart to count as one flock. The ברייתא says a single animal in ציפורי, in between, joins them. If one animal is enough, רב's demand for five in the middle looks wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection (usually from a ברייתא or משנה)
They join together to make up the count
ציפורי, a town located between the two villages

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
If he had five in the village of Chananya
and five in the village of Otnai,
they do not combine
unless he has one in Tzippori.
phrases.notes: ציפורי lies between the two villages.

phrases.english: This is a refutation of Rav!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב's position from the earlier part of the sugya.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that five animals are needed in the middle
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says a single animal in the middle joins the two groups, so five should not be required.

steps.title: שמואל explains the ברייתא in a way that fits רב
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says the ברייתא means nine on each side with one in the middle. That one animal can complete ten for either side.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל explained it according to רב: The case is where there were nine here, nine there, and one in the middle. That one is fit to count with this side and fit to count with that side.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל defends רב by reinterpreting the case in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In שמואל's reading, the middle animal does not join two groups of five. Each side has nine, and the middle animal is close enough to either side to make ten. So the ברייתא does not prove that one animal joins distant flocks, and רב survives.
steps.confusionAlert: שמואל himself disagrees with רב. Here he is only showing that the ברייתא can be read to fit רב. He is not giving up his own view.

phrases.english: Shmuel interpreted it according to Rav:
for example, where there were nine from here
and nine from there and one in the middle,
for that one is fit to go with here
and fit to go with there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the case in the ברייתא (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא means five on each side are joined by one animal in the middle.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means nine on each side. The middle animal can complete ten for either side, so it says nothing against רב.

steps.title: רב פפא: according to שמואל, even the shepherd or his tools join the flocks
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא extends שמואל's view. Even the shepherd standing in the middle, or just his tools left there, joins the two flocks.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: According to שמואל, even the shepherd joins them, and even the shepherd's tools join them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא draws out how far שמואל's view reaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שמואל, the middle animal works because the shepherd must go there, which links the two sides. By that logic the shepherd himself in the middle is enough. Even his tools are enough, since he will have to go back to get them.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: And according to Shmuel,
even the shepherd combines them,
and even the shepherd's implements combine them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defending רב to working out how far שמואל's view goes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to שמואל, a shepherd or even his tools in the middle joins two distant flocks.

steps.title: רב אשי asks about the shepherd's dog
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks whether the shepherd's dog in the middle joins the flocks. Maybe it does not, since the shepherd can just call it. Or maybe it does, since sometimes it won't come and he must go get it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי asked: What about the shepherd's dog? Since he calls it and it comes, perhaps the flocks do not join. Or perhaps they do, since sometimes it does not come and he himself has to go and bring it?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי builds on רב פפא's rule and asks whether a dog is like the shepherd's tools.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test from step 3 is whether the shepherd will need to walk to the middle. A dog usually comes when called, so he would not need to go. But dogs sometimes don't listen, and then he would have to go after it.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked a question he did not know the answer to

phrases.english: Rav Ashi asked:
What about the shepherd's dog?
Since he calls it and it comes,
they do not combine;
or perhaps sometimes it does not come,
and he himself needs to go and bring it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רב פפא's rule to a borderline case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the shepherd's dog in the middle join two distant flocks, the way his tools do?

steps.title: The question about the dog is left unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends with תיקו, meaning רב אשי's question stays open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the discussion with no answer to the dog question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither side of רב אשי's question is decided. Both reasons, that the dog comes when called and that it sometimes doesn't, are left standing.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand (the question remains unresolved)

steps.whatToRemember: רב needs five animals in the middle to join distant flocks; שמואל needs only one. The ברייתא can be read to fit רב (nine on each side, one in the middle). According to שמואל, even the shepherd or his tools join the flocks. Whether his dog does is a תיקו.

phrases.english: Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes רב אשי's question without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whether the shepherd's dog joins the flocks remains an unresolved question.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: the Jordan separates flocks
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי מאיר's rule from the משנה that the יַרְדֵּן divides flocks for מעשר בהמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: The Jordan River separates flocks with regard to animal tithe.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. This sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, flocks close enough together join to make ten for מעשר בהמה. רבי מאיר says the יַרְדֵּן breaks that joining, even if the flocks are very close. The question coming next is why.

keyTerms.meaning: Animal tithe: every tenth animal is set aside

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says:
The Jordan separates with regard to animal tithe.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: הַיַּרְדֵּן מַפְסִיק לְמַעְשַׂר בְּהֵמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New section. After the open תיקו, the גמרא moves to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The יַרְדֵּן separates flocks for מעשר בהמה.

steps.title: רבי אמי: a bridge joins the flocks
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי limits רבי מאיר's rule to a place with no bridge. A bridge joins the two flocks.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי said: They only taught this where there is no bridge. But if there is a bridge, the bridge joins the flocks.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי adds a limit to רבי מאיר's rule. The יַרְדֵּן only separates the flocks when there is no bridge across it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי אמי, the river divides only when there is no way across. Once a bridge connects the two sides, the flocks count as one group again.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this in the case of...

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין שָׁם גֶּשֶׁר,
phrases.english: They only taught this where there is no bridge there,
but if there is a bridge there,
the bridge joins them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַמֵּי: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין שָׁם גֶּשֶׁר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבי מאיר's rule to a case with no bridge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The יַרְדֵּן separates flocks only where there is no bridge. A bridge joins them.

steps.title: The reason seems to be distance
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes from רבי אמי that the reason the יַרְדֵּן separates is that the flocks cannot reach each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: So it seems the reason is that the flocks are not close to each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion about the reason behind the rule. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a bridge fixes the problem, then the problem must be physical: the animals cannot get to each other. Now the גמרא will test whether this reason really holds.

keyTerms.meaning: They are close (can reach each other)

phrases.english: Apparently, it is because they are not close together.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Works out the reason implied by רבי אמי's bridge rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The reason the יַרְדֵּן divides is that the flocks cannot physically reach each other.

steps.title: A ברייתא: different regions do not join
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that flocks on two sides of the יַרְדֵּן, or in two districts, do not join. Certainly flocks in חוץ לארץ and in ארץ ישראל do not join.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: If someone had flocks on both sides of the Jordan, here and there, or in two districts such as Namer and Namori, they do not join. And it goes without saying that flocks outside the Land and in the Land do not join.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge the idea that the reason is distance. The point of the challenge is spelled out in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists cases where flocks do not join, and none of them depends on a physical block. Its strongest case is flocks in חוץ לארץ and in ארץ ישראל.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection (usually from a ברייתא)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:

phrases.aramaic: הָיוּ לוֹ בִּשְׁנֵי עֶבְרֵי הַיַּרְדֵּן אֵילָךְ וְאֵילָךְ,
phrases.english: If he had flocks on the two sides of the Jordan, here and there,
or in two districts,
such as Namer and Namori,
they do not join,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר חוּצָה לָאָרֶץ וָאָרֶץ.
phrases.english: and it goes without saying outside the Land and the Land.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: הָיוּ לוֹ בִּשְׁנֵי עֶבְרֵי הַיַּרְדֵּן אֵילָךְ וְאֵילָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to test the distance reason from step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the יַרְדֵּן separates only because the flocks cannot reach each other (רבי אמי's bridge rule).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says flocks in חוץ לארץ and in ארץ ישראל do not join, even though no river separates them. Step 10 spells this out.

steps.title: The Land's border is like having a bridge
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the border of ארץ ישראל is like a place with a bridge, yet the ברייתא says the flocks do not join.
steps.simpleTranslation: But outside the Land and the Land are like a place that has a bridge, and yet the ברייתא teaches that they do not join!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains exactly why the ברייתא is a problem. The flocks can walk across this border, yet they still do not join.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing physically blocks the animals at the border of ארץ ישראל, so it is just like having a bridge. Still, the flocks do not join. So the dividing line must be a legal border, not a physical block, and the distance reason does not hold up.

phrases.english: But outside the Land and the Land
are like a place that has a bridge,
and yet it teaches: they do not join!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא חוּצָה לָאָרֶץ וָאָרֶץ כִּמְקוֹם שֶׁיֵּשׁ גֶּשֶׁר דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the point of the ברייתא from step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The distance reason drawn from רבי אמי.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Flocks can cross the border of ארץ ישראל, which is just like having a bridge. Yet they do not join. So a physical crossing does not decide whether flocks join.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the Jordan is a border by פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the distance reason. רבי יוחנן explains that a פסוק makes the יַרְדֵּן a border in its own right.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: This is רבי מאיר's reason. The verse says, 'And the Jordan shall border it on the east side.' The Torah made the Jordan a border in its own right.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up its earlier reason and offers a new one. The יַרְדֵּן divides because the פסוק calls it a border.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אֶלָּא drops the inference from step 8, which the ברייתא just disproved. In its place, רבי חייא בר אבא gives a different reason: the יַרְדֵּן divides because the Torah names it a border, not because animals cannot cross it. On this reason a bridge should not matter, just as with the border of ארץ ישראל. רבי אמי's view is not erased, though. Step 16 sets the two views side by side.

keyTerms.meaning: A border in its own right

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי חייא בר אבא in the name of רבי יוחנן, רבי מאיר's rule is not about distance. The יַרְדֵּן is a border set by the פסוק, so even a bridge would not join the flocks across it.
steps.confusionAlert: The אֶלָּא drops the גמרא's own inference ('אלמא...'), not רבי אמי as a person. From here on there are two competing explanations of רבי מאיר: רבי אמי (physical separation, so a bridge joins the flocks) and רבי חייא בר אבא (a border set by a פסוק). Step 16 returns to challenge רבי אמי.
steps.whyThisMatters: This changes the kind of rule we are dealing with. The יַרְדֵּן is a legal border, not just a physical obstacle.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
This is the reason of Rabbi Meir,
for the verse says:
"And the Jordan shall border it on the east side" (Joshua 18:20),
the verse made it a border in its own right.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: הַיְינוּ טַעְמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by dropping the distance reason and replacing it with a reason from a פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Retraction and new reason: the rule now comes from a פסוק, not from distance.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The יַרְדֵּן divides because the flocks cannot reach each other, so a bridge would join them.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק makes the יַרְדֵּן its own border. It divides like the border of ארץ ישראל, even with a bridge.

steps.title: Should tribal borders also split the flocks?
steps.stepSummary: If a פסוק calling a place a border makes it a separate border, then the tribal boundaries in ספר יהושע should also split flocks for מעשר בהמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, look at the פסוקים 'And the border was drawn' and 'And the border went up.' Here too the פסוק makes each one a border by itself!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 11. If a פסוק calling the יַרְדֵּן a border makes it a separate border, then the tribal borders, which are also described in פסוקים, should separate flocks as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 11 was that a פסוק makes the יַרְדֵּן a border. But ספר יהושע also uses border language for the lines between each tribe's land. So the rule seems to prove too much: flocks in two different tribes' areas would never join for מעשר בהמה.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so, now (introduces a challenge from the previous answer)
A border by itself, a separate border

phrases.english: But if so, now,
'And the border was drawn,' 'And the border went up,'
phrases.notes: These are פסוקים in ספר יהושע describing the tribal boundaries.

phrases.english: here too the verse made it
a border by itself!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the תירוץ of step 11 by pushing its logic further.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a פסוק makes the יַרְדֵּן a border in its own right.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'a פסוק calls it a border' is enough, the tribal borders should also split the flocks. That is unacceptable.

steps.title: All of ארץ ישראל counts as one border
steps.stepSummary: The tribal borders are different, because a פסוק teaches that all of ארץ ישראל is one border.
steps.simpleTranslation: There it is different, because the פסוק says: 'This shall be your land according to its borders round about.' All of ארץ ישראל is one border.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Another פסוק joins all the land inside ארץ ישראל into one unit, so the inner tribal lines do not split flocks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tribal borders are real lines, but the פסוק in במדבר treats the whole land as one bordered unit. So for מעשר בהמה, the tribal lines do not create separate areas.

keyTerms.meaning: 'According to its borders round about' (במדבר לד:יב)

phrases.english: There it is different, for the verse says:
'This shall be your land
according to its borders round about,'

phrases.aramaic: כּוּלַּהּ אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל גְּבוּל אֶחָד הִיא.
phrases.english: all of the Land of Israel is one border.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction based on a separate פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The tribal borders, like the יַרְדֵּן, should split the flocks.
steps.terutzMaskana: A פסוק joins all of ארץ ישראל into one border, so the tribal lines inside it do not split flocks.

steps.title: Then the יַרְדֵּן should be included too
steps.stepSummary: If all of ארץ ישראל is one border, the יַרְדֵּן should also be swallowed into that single border.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the יַרְדֵּן too should not separate!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer it just gave. If the whole land is one border, why should the יַרְדֵּן still separate flocks?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'one border' פסוק seems to cancel every inner division, and the יַרְדֵּן is also inside the larger territory. So the new answer appears to undo the original rule about the יַרְדֵּן.

phrases.english: If so, the Jordan too [should not divide]!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the תירוץ of step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that all of ארץ ישראל is one border.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If everything is one border, the יַרְדֵּן should also be included, which goes against the rule that it separates.

steps.title: The פסוק says 'land', not river
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says 'land', so it joins only connected land. The יַרְדֵּן is water, not land.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Land', and not the יַרְדֵּן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers from the exact wording of the פסוק. The word 'land' covers only land, so a river like the יַרְדֵּן keeps its own status as a border.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'one border' rule is limited to areas joined by land. The יַרְדֵּן is a river, so it is not included in that joining, and it still splits the flocks.

keyTerms.meaning: Land (the key word in the פסוק)

phrases.english: 'Land' and not the Jordan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Precise reading of a word in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'one border' rule includes the יַרְדֵּן too.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only land is joined into one border. The יַרְדֵּן, a river, stays a separate border.
steps.whatToRemember: According to this approach: tribal lines inside ארץ ישראל do not split flocks, because the whole land is one border. The יַרְדֵּן does split them, because a פסוק calls it a border and it is not 'land'.

steps.title: Why only the יַרְדֵּן according to רבי אמי?
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא's פסוק-based approach explains why the יַרְדֵּן alone is named. Under רבי אמי's distance-based reason, every river the flocks cannot cross should have been named.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works well for רבי חייא בר אבא: that is why the יַרְדֵּן is taught. But according to רבי אמי, let it teach all rivers!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now returns to the two explanations of רבי מאיר's rule and challenges רבי אמי. If the reason is only that the animals cannot cross, why did רבי מאיר mention only the יַרְדֵּן?
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי חייא בר אבא, the יַרְדֵּן is special because of a פסוק, so naming it alone makes sense. For רבי אמי, the reason is physical separation, and that applies to any river that cannot be crossed. Then singling out the יַרְדֵּן seems pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: It works well for (introduces a contrast between two views)

phrases.english: It works well according to Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba:
that is why it teaches 'the Jordan,'
phrases.notes: Because a פסוק shows that the יַרְדֵּן is special.

phrases.english: but according to Rabbi Ami,
let it teach all rivers!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defending the פסוק approach to challenging רבי אמי's approach from steps 7-8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אמי's reason that the יַרְדֵּן separates because the flocks cannot reach each other.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reason applies to every river that cannot be crossed, so naming only the יַרְדֵּן makes no sense.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two views. רבי חייא בר אבא says the יַרְדֵּן is a border because of a פסוק. רבי אמי says it separates because the animals cannot cross it. This challenge hits only רבי אמי.

steps.title: The challenge on רבי אמי stands
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves the question on רבי אמי unanswered.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits it has no answer to the challenge against רבי אמי, and the question stays open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קשיא means the question is strong and unresolved. It is weaker than a full refutation (תיובתא), but רבי אמי's view is left with a real difficulty.

keyTerms.meaning: It is difficult (the question remains unanswered)

phrases.english: It is difficult.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the challenge of step 16 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פסוק-based explanation of רבי חייא בר אבא holds up. רבי אמי's distance-based explanation is left with an unresolved difficulty.
steps.whatToRemember: Final picture: the יַרְדֵּן splits flocks for מעשר בהמה because a פסוק makes it a border, and it is not 'land'. The inner tribal lines do not split flocks. רבי אמי's view remains difficult.

steps.title: Suggesting a dispute of תנאים: the first opinion says the יַרְדֵּן is not ארץ כנען
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that whether the יַרְדֵּן counts as 'land' is a dispute between תנאים. It brings רבי יהודה בן בתירה, who learns from the word 'ארצה' that the יַרְדֵּן is not ארץ כנען.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say this is a dispute between תנאים. The פסוק says: 'When you cross the יַרְדֵּן into the land of Canaan.' 'Into the land' means the land of Canaan, and the יַרְדֵּן is not the land of Canaan. These are the words of רבי יהודה בן בתירה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proposes that the earlier claim, that the יַרְדֵּן is water and not 'land', may be a dispute between תנאים. It brings the first side of that dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 said the single border of ארץ ישראל joins only land, and the יַרְדֵּן is water. Here רבי יהודה בן בתירה reads the פסוק as separating 'crossing the יַרְדֵּן' from 'arriving in ארץ כנען'. That reading fits the idea that the יַרְדֵּן is not part of the land.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say it is like a dispute between תנאים. The גמרא suggests that an idea of the אמוראים depends on an argument between תנאים.
A תנא who holds that the יַרְדֵּן is not ארץ כנען

steps.confusionAlert: 'לימא כתנאי' is only a suggestion. The גמרא is proposing a link to a dispute between תנאים. It is not stating a final ruling.

phrases.english: Let us say it is like a dispute of Tannaim:
"When you cross the Jordan
into the land of Canaan"
"Into the land" means the land of Canaan,
but the Jordan is not the land of Canaan;
these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the unanswered question on רבי אמי, the גמרא returns to the idea from step 15 and suggests it depends on a dispute between תנאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה בן בתירה, the יַרְדֵּן is not part of ארץ כנען.

steps.title: The second opinion: the יַרְדֵּן is part of ארץ כנען, like ירחו
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן יוחי brings a different פסוק, which links the יַרְדֵּן with ירחו. Just as ירחו is ארץ כנען, so is the יַרְדֵּן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן יוחי says: The פסוק says 'beyond the יַרְדֵּן of ירחו, eastward toward the sunrise.' Just as ירחו is the land of Canaan, the יַרְדֵּן is also the land of Canaan.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the other side of the dispute between the תנאים. רבי שמעון בן יוחי holds that the יַרְדֵּן is part of ארץ כנען.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק joins the two names into 'יַרְדֵּן ירחו'. רבי שמעון בן יוחי treats them as alike: since ירחו is clearly in ארץ כנען, the יַרְדֵּן is too. In this view, the יַרְדֵּן would not be an outsider to the land.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who holds that the יַרְדֵּן is ארץ כנען
Just as ... so too. This is a comparison formula.

steps.whatToRemember: There is a dispute between תנאים about the יַרְדֵּן. רבי יהודה בן בתירה says it is not ארץ כנען. רבי שמעון בן יוחי says it is, like ירחו.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says:
Behold, the verse says:
"Beyond the Jordan of Jericho
eastward, toward the sunrise";
just as Jericho is the land of Canaan,
so too the Jordan is the land of Canaan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the dispute between the תנאים by bringing the opposing view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי שמעון בן יוחי, the יַרְדֵּן is part of ארץ כנען, because the פסוק links it with ירחו.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the river is only called יַרְדֵּן from בית ירחו and south
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה quotes רבי יוחנן: the name 'יַרְדֵּן' only applies from בית ירחו and further south.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: It is only called 'יַרְדֵּן' from בית ירחו and below.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement begins. רבי יוחנן defines which part of the river officially counts as 'the יַרְדֵּן'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The river flows a long way before it reaches ירחו. רבי יוחנן says only the southern section, from בית ירחו down, carries the official name 'יַרְדֵּן'. The גמרא will next ask what practical difference this makes.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who transmits teachings of רבי יוחנן
From בית ירחו and below, meaning southward

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
It is not called "Jordan" except
from Beit Jericho and below.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new statement that defines the term 'יַרְדֵּן' geographically.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name 'יַרְדֵּן' applies only from בית ירחו southward.

steps.title: For which הלכה does this matter?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical law depends on רבי יוחנן's definition.
steps.simpleTranslation: For what הלכה is this said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why this definition matters in practice. This sets up the next move, where it tries out possible answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A place-name definition needs a practical use. The גמרא looks for the הלכה where it makes a difference whether a stretch of river is called 'יַרְדֵּן'.

keyTerms.meaning: For what הלכה? It asks for the practical relevance of a statement.

phrases.english: For what halacha is this relevant?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical purpose of רבי יוחנן's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which הלכה depends on where the river starts being called 'יַרְדֵּן'?

steps.title: It cannot be about vows, since vows follow ordinary speech
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the rule might be about נדרים, then rejects that idea. Vows follow how people actually talk, so wherever people call the river 'יַרְדֵּן', the vow applies.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is for someone who makes a vow, we follow the language of people. So anywhere people call it 'יַרְדֵּן', it would be forbidden to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests one possible answer, a person who vows not to use יַרְדֵּן water, and rejects it right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In נדרים, words mean what ordinary people mean by them. Since people call the river 'יַרְדֵּן' even north of ירחו, a vow would include those areas too. So רבי יוחנן's narrow definition cannot be about vows.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say. This introduces a suggestion that is about to be rejected.
Follow the language of people. In vows, words mean what they mean in common speech.

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a general rule: in נדרים, the common meaning of words counts, not a technical definition.

phrases.english: If you say it is for one who vows,
we follow the language of people,
and anywhere that they call it "Jordan"
it is forbidden to him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries one answer to the question of step 21 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that רבי יוחנן's definition is about vows.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Vows follow common speech, and people call the whole river 'יַרְדֵּן'. A technical definition would therefore make no difference for vows.

steps.title: Rather, it matters for animal tithe
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that רבי יוחנן's definition matters for מעשר בהמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is for מעשר בהמה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its real answer: the definition matters for מעשר בהמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For מעשר בהמה, the question is whether the יַרְדֵּן separates flocks so they cannot be counted together. The answer here is that only the stretch officially called 'יַרְדֵּן', from בית ירחו south, has that status.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. This introduces the correct answer after a rejected one.
Animal tithe. Every tenth animal is set aside.

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן's rule, that it is only 'יַרְדֵּן' from בית ירחו down, applies to מעשר בהמה. It does not apply to vows.

phrases.english: Rather, it is for animal tithe.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the correct answer after the vow suggestion was rejected.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The definition matters for מעשר בהמה. There, only the stretch called 'יַרְדֵּן' has the special status as a separator.

steps.title: A ברייתא traces the river's path and supports רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא follows the river from מערת פמייס through the lakes to the Great Sea. It ends by stating the same rule as רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא also teaches this: The יַרְדֵּן comes out of מערת פמייס, flows through the sea of סיבכי, the sea of טבריא, and the sea of סדום, and continues and falls into the Great Sea. But it is only called 'יַרְדֵּן' from בית יריחו and below.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says exactly what רבי יוחנן said, as support.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא admits the river is one long body of water starting far to the north. Still, it limits the official name 'יַרְדֵּן' to the stretch from בית יריחו south. This matches רבי יוחנן word for word.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also taught this way in a ברייתא. This introduces support.
The cave of Pamyas, the river's source
The sea of Sivchi, a northern lake

phrases.english: It is also taught so in a baraita:
The Jordan issues from the Cave of Pamyas,
and flows through the Sea of Sivchi,
and through the Sea of Tiberias,
and through the Sea of Sodom,
and continues and falls into the Great Sea;
but it is not called "Jordan" except from Beit Jericho and below.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי יוחנן's statement from step 20 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's rule that the name 'יַרְדֵּן' starts only at בית ירחו.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that traces the river's whole path and states the same rule.

steps.title: Why the river is called יַרְדֵּן
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא quotes רבי יוחנן: the name יַרְדֵּן comes from 'יורד מדן', meaning it goes down from דן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Why is the river called 'יַרְדֵּן'? Because it goes down (יורד) from דן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching of רבי יוחנן about the יַרְדֵּן, this time explaining where its name comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word יַרְדֵּן is read as two parts: 'ירד', meaning goes down, and 'דן', the city or territory of the tribe of דן. The name itself tells us the river begins in דן's area and flows downward from there.

keyTerms.meaning: the city/territory of the tribe of Dan in the far north

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said
Rabbi Yochanan said:
Why is its name called "Yarden"?
Because it goes down from Dan.
phrases.notes: A play on the word: יורד (goes down) + דן.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second teaching of רבי יוחנן about the יַרְדֵּן, after his rule about where the name applies (Step 20).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name יַרְדֵּן means 'descends from דן'; the river starts in דן's territory.

steps.title: Another school learns it from a verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא tells רב אשי: you learn that the river starts in דן from its name, but we learn it from a פסוק saying לשם was renamed דן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said to רב אשי: You learn this from there (from the river's name). We learn it from here: 'And they called לשם "דן", after the name of דן their father' (יהושע יט:מז).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא offers a different source for the idea that the יַרְדֵּן starts in דן. This step begins a chain of proof that the next step finishes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reading the name is one way to learn the fact. רבי אבא's school uses a פסוק instead: the tribe of דן captured a city called לשם and renamed it דן. On its own the פסוק says nothing about the river, so we still need to link לשם to the river's source.

keyTerms.meaning: you (your school) learn it from there
a city captured by the tribe of דן and renamed דן

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said to Rav Ashi:
You learn it from there (from the name),
we learn it from here:
"And they called Leshem: Dan,
after the name of Dan their father."

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתּוּן מֵהָתָם מַתְנִיתוּ לַהּ, אֲנַן מֵהָכָא מַתְנֵינַן לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different source (a פסוק) for the same fact that Step 25 learned from the river's name.
steps.raayaObject: That the יַרְדֵּן begins in the territory of דן
steps.raayaSupportSource: יהושע יט:מז, where לשם is renamed דן

steps.title: לשם is פמייס, where the יַרְדֵּן begins
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק says לשם is פמייס, and a ברייתא says the יַרְדֵּן comes out of the cave of פמייס. This completes the proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יצחק said: לשם is פמייס. And a ברייתא teaches: the יַרְדֵּן comes out of the cave of פמייס.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבי אבא's chain of proof by connecting the city in the פסוק to the actual start of the river.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three links. First, the פסוק says לשם became דן. Second, רבי יצחק says לשם is the place later called פמייס. Third, the ברייתא says the יַרְדֵּן starts in the cave of פמייס. Together they show the river begins in דן.

keyTerms.meaning: Pamyas (Paneas / Banias), the later name of לשם
the cave of Pamyas, where the יַרְדֵּן begins
it was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak said:
Leshem is Pamyas,
and it was taught (in a baraita):
The Jordan comes out of the Cave of Pamyas.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: לֶשֶׁם זוֹ פַּמְיָיס, וְתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the missing links that turn the פסוק from Step 26 into a proof about the river.
steps.raayaObject: That the יַרְדֵּן starts in דן (in לשם / פמייס)
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יצחק's identification of לשם as פמייס, together with the ברייתא that the יַרְדֵּן comes out of the cave of פמייס
steps.whatToRemember: פסוק (לשם became דן) + רבי יצחק (לשם is פמייס) + ברייתא (the יַרְדֵּן starts at פמייס) = the יַרְדֵּן starts in דן.

steps.title: A vow on the source forbids the whole river
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא says the source of the יַרְדֵּן is the cave of פמייס. So someone who vows not to drink water from that cave may not drink from any part of the יַרְדֵּן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: The source of the יַרְדֵּן is the cave of פמייס. So if someone says 'I will not drink water from the cave of פמייס', he is forbidden to drink from the whole יַרְדֵּן.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא gives a practical law based on the fact that the river starts at פמייס. This is the first of three 'source' (זכרותא) teachings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All the water of the יַרְדֵּן flows out of that cave. So a person who forbids himself the cave's water is understood to have forbidden all the water that comes from it, meaning the entire river.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't confuse this with Step 22, which said vows follow how people normally talk. Here the person named the river's source. People understand that the source includes all the water flowing from it, so the vow covers the whole river.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
The source of the Jordan is from the Cave of Pamyas,
so where one said:
"I will not drink water from the Cave of Pamyas,"
it is forbidden to him in the entire Jordan.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא: זַכְרוּתֵיהּ דְּיַרְדְּנָא מִמְּעָרַת פַּמְיָיס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the fact proven in Step 27 (the river starts at פמייס) and draws a law about vows from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow against water from the cave of פמייס forbids drinking from the entire יַרְדֵּן.

steps.title: The liver is the source of blood
steps.stepSummary: The source of blood is the liver. This fits רבי יצחק's rule that a dissolved liver of a dead body makes things טמא in the amount of a רביעית, just like blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: The source of blood is the liver. This matches רבי יצחק, who said: A liver that dissolved makes things טמא with a רביעית.
steps.whatsHappening: The second 'source' teaching: the liver is the source of blood. The גמרא shows its practical law through רבי יצחק's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Blood from a dead person makes things טמא if there is a רביעית of it. Since the liver is basically the 'root' of blood, a liver that melted into liquid counts as blood. So a רביעית of it also makes things טמא.

keyTerms.meaning: a quarter-לוג, the amount of a dead person's blood that makes things טמא

phrases.english: The source of blood is the liver,
in line with Rabbi Yitzchak,
as Rabbi Yitzchak said:
A liver that dissolved
makes things impure with a quarter-log.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second in רב כהנא's series of 'source' teachings, moving from rivers to blood.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The liver is the source of blood, so a dissolved liver of a dead body makes things טמא with a רביעית, like blood.

steps.title: The Euphrates is the source of all water
steps.stepSummary: The source of all water is the פרת. So, as רב יהודה quoted רב, someone who vows against the water of the פרת is forbidden to drink any water in the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: The source of water is the פרת. As רב יהודה said in the name of רב: Someone who vows against the water of the פרת is forbidden to drink all the water in the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The third and last 'source' teaching: the פרת is the source of all water, and the practical law is about vows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works the same way as the cave of פמייס in Step 28. Since the פרת is seen as the root of all water, a vow against its water reaches every body of water that comes from it, which means all water in the world.
steps.whatToRemember: רב כהנא's three 'sources' (זכרותא): the cave of פמייס is the source of the יַרְדֵּן (vows), the liver is the source of blood (טומאה), and the פרת is the source of all water (vows). In each case, what applies to the source applies to whatever comes from it.

phrases.english: The source of water is the Euphrates,
as Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
One who vows against the waters of the Euphrates
is forbidden to drink from all the waters in the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: זַכְרוּתָא דְּמַיָּא — פְּרָת, דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the series of three 'source' teachings, returning to vows like the first one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow against the water of the פרת forbids all water in the world, since the פרת is the source of all water.

steps.title: What exact vow forbids all water?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the previous rule is talking about.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what exact case the previous rule about the פרת is talking about. This question sets up the next steps, which try out possible answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 30 said that a person who vows against the water of the פרת may not drink any water in the world. That is a very broad result, so the גמרא wants to know which wording of the vow leads to it.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the circumstances?

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
phrases.notes: Asks about the case in Step 30: the vow that forbids all water.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what kind of vow is meant by the rule stated in Step 30.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact wording of a vow that would forbid every kind of water in the world.

steps.title: Saying 'water of the פרת' only forbids that one river
steps.stepSummary: If he only said 'I won't drink the water of the פרת,' only the פרת is forbidden, and other rivers are allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the case is where he said 'I will not drink from the water of the פרת,' that can't be right. In that case only the water of the פרת is forbidden to him, and he may drink from another river.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the simplest wording of the vow and rejects it. 'The water of the פרת' means only that river.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vows follow the way people normally talk. When people say 'the water of the פרת,' they mean only the river itself, not water that flows out from it far away. So this wording cannot be the case that forbids all water.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion that is about to be rejected)

steps.confusionAlert: Even though the water of all rivers really does come from the פרת (as the next steps explain), the plain words 'water of the פרת' still mean only that one river. In vows, normal speech is what counts, not geography.

phrases.english: If we say it is where he said:
phrases.notes: The first suggestion, which will be rejected.

phrases.english: 'I will not drink from the water of the Euphrates' —
it is only the Euphrates water that I won't drink,
phrases.notes: This is how his words would be understood.

phrases.english: but from another river I do drink.
phrases.notes: So other water stays allowed, which doesn't fit the rule in Step 30.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers one possible answer to the question in Step 31 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the vow wording 'the water of the פרת' forbids all water.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: In normal speech, that wording means only the river itself, so other rivers stay allowed.

steps.title: The vow must say 'water that comes from the פרת'
steps.stepSummary: The real case is where he vowed not to drink any water that comes from the פרת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the case is where he said: 'I will not drink from water that comes from the פרת.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its real answer. The vow forbids all water because he said 'water that comes from the פרת.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: This wording does not point only to the river itself. It includes any water that started in the פרת. So the question now becomes which water starts there, and the next step answers that.

phrases.english: Rather, it is where he said:
'I will not drink from water that comes from the Euphrates,'
phrases.notes: Includes any water whose source is the פרת.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected suggestion in Step 32 with the correct case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The vow forbids all water when he says 'water that comes from the פרת', since that includes any water that started in the פרת.

steps.title: All rivers get their water from the פרת
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches that all rivers get their water from three rivers, and those three get theirs from the פרת. So all water 'comes from the פרת.'
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב יהודה said in the name of רב: all the rivers are below three rivers (they get their water from them), and the three rivers are below the פרת (they get their water from it).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support from רב to explain why 'water that comes from the פרת' includes all water in the world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב describes a chain: every river is fed by three main rivers, and those three are fed by the פרת. So all river water first came from the פרת. That is why this vow forbids every kind of water, which matches the rule in Step 30.

keyTerms.meaning: רב יהודה quoting his teacher רב
Below; here it means getting water from
Three rivers (the other rivers of Eden, in בראשית ב)

steps.whatToRemember: A vow against 'the water of the פרת' forbids only that river. A vow against 'water that comes from the פרת' forbids all water, because according to רב all rivers start from the פרת.

phrases.english: As Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
All the rivers are below the three rivers,
phrases.notes: They get their water from the three rivers of Eden (פישון, גיחון, חדקל).

phrases.english: and the three rivers are below the Euphrates.
phrases.notes: So in the end, all water comes from the פרת.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the wording in Step 33 includes all water.
steps.raayaObject: That 'water that comes from the פרת' covers all water in the world.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב יהודה quoting רב: all rivers come from three rivers, and the three come from the פרת.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is where the 'source' idea pays off in practice. A vow that names the source of something also covers everything that flows from that source.

steps.title: A challenge begins: 'But there are'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts asking a question against רב's statement. The rest of the question continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there are...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a challenge with 'וְהָאִיכָּא' ('but there are'). This only sets up the next move; the full question continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'וְהָאִיכָּא' usually introduces a counterexample: something that seems not to fit the rule that was just stated. Here it seems to be pointing to water that does not come from the פרת, which would challenge רב's claim that all rivers come from it.

phrases.english: But there are
phrases.notes: The challenge continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts to challenge רב's claim in Step 34 that all rivers come from the פרת.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's statement that all rivers get their water from the פרת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It points to a counterexample that seems not to come from the פרת. The details continue on the next amud.
